A_serious.english: If that were to arise together with the mind in a manner similar to faculties such as the eye
A_serious.problem: The Tibetan says pleasure arises together with the mind from the SAME causes (eye etc.), which is the whole point of the verse's རྒྱུ་མཚུངས་པ; A turns it into a likeness to the eye-faculty, so the shared-cause argument drops out.

B_serious.english: These are the causes for the mind not being direct.
B_serious.problem: The Tibetan says perceived pleasure etc. is the cause/ground of the non-perceptible mind (the thing to be inferred). B says pleasure causes the mind to be non-direct, which distorts the opponent's claim.

pages.note: Both translations follow the self-cognition argument and both verses closely; each has one misconstrued clause in the commentary on the second verse.

B_serious.english: whatever entity lacks invariable absence in the absence of the probandum
B_serious.problem: The text as printed says the entity 'is absent when the probandum is absent' (med na med pa). B adds 'lacks', which reverses that clause. A renders it literally.

pages.note: Both are close to the image throughout the five-objects and two-perceptibles verses; only B adds a negation to the final commentary clause.

Both render the unseen-sign verse, the infinite-regress verse and the arthāpatti/presence exchange correctly; A's verse line 'How can evidence be understood?' gets the object of rtogs wrong (it should be the mind), but its commentary fixes it, so the error is minor.
